title: Streaming in Spark: Structured Streaming and watermarks
goal: By the end, you can read a streaming query in Spark as this track's ideas in new words, predict when a count with a watermark is written and which late payments it drops, pick an output mode for where the results go, say what makes the path from Kafka to an Iceberg table exactly-once, and explain what Spark's real-time mode gains in speed and gives up in guarantees.
opening:
Picture a café's card reader on a busy morning. Each tap sends a payment to the payments app, stamped with the time the card was used. A program counts each shop's payments in every five minutes, so a sudden burst stands out, like a stolen card tried again and again.

At 10:14, a payment stamped 10:03 turns up. The reader had lost its Wi-Fi and kept the payment until it came back. The count for 10:00 to 10:05 is nine minutes old. Should it change?

It's tempting to close each count when its five minutes are up. That's what a person with a stopwatch would do, but the clock says nothing about payments still on their way.

In Fault tolerance in stream processing: checkpoints and exactly-once, small batches made a crashed program safe to restart. In this lesson, we'll run the count in Spark, which works in those batches. We'll watch it decide when a count is finished, choose how results are written, and crash it between two writes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The program from the opening counts payments per shop in 5-minute windows of the time each card was used. It's told to accept latecomers up to 10 minutes behind the newest payment it has seen. The newest payment so far is from 10:14. A payment stamped 10:03 arrives now. What happens to it?
options: Dropped: it's 11 minutes behind the newest payment, more than the 10 minutes allowed
Counted in its own window, 10:00 to 10:05, because that window is still open
Counted in the current window, 10:10 to 10:15
The program stops with an error about late data
warmup.why: Spark's watermark is the newest event time seen minus the delay: 10:14 minus 10 minutes is 10:04. Spark drops a late payment only once its window has closed, meaning the watermark has reached the window's end. The window from 10:00 to 10:05 ends at 10:05, after 10:04, so it's still open and the payment is counted. The tempting first option judges the payment by its own age, which isn't Spark's rule. The stepper in the second section shows this exact batch.

sections.h: Spark runs your query again on each small batch of new payments
sections.body:
Let's put the count from the opening into a real engine. Lessons 4 to 7 of this track built stream processing from ideas that don't belong to any one tool: event time and watermarks, state, joins, and getting through a crash. This lesson tries them out in the engine you're most likely to meet wherever companies keep large amounts of data. Apache Spark is a free program that runs data jobs on many machines at once. Its part for streams is called **Structured Streaming**. The labs use Spark 4.1; 4.3 is the newest release.

Spark began as a batch engine, a tool for jobs that work through a fixed pile of data, and its streaming keeps that shape. A program called the driver turns your query into a plan. Programs called executors, on other machines, run the plan as tasks, one per partition (a slice of the data), side by side. A count per shop needs all of a shop's rows in one task, so Spark first moves rows between tasks by key, a step called a shuffle. The Batch track builds this engine properly; that's all you need here.

You write the query against a DataFrame, Spark's name for a table of rows with named columns that your code can filter, group and count. Structured Streaming treats the input stream as a table that keeps getting new rows, and your query describes a result table over it. Spark doesn't work out the whole result again each time. It runs in **micro-batches**, lesson 7's first fix. At every trigger, the moment Spark starts a new batch (by default, as soon as the previous one finishes), it asks the source for the data that's new since last time. With Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, that means the new offsets, the positions in the log. Then Spark runs the plan on only those rows and combines the result with what it remembered.

Here's the count from the opening. The labs' tables call a shop a merchant, and the code calls a card payment an authorization, the moment the card's bank says yes. Event time is when the card was used, as stamped in the payment; processing time is when the program reads it. A window is a slice of event time, such as 10:00 to 10:05, and tumbling windows sit back to back without overlapping. The rule counts payments per shop in 5-minute tumbling windows of event time, written as the same `groupBy` you'd write over a table (it gathers the rows that share a window and a shop):

```kotlin
events.groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id")).count()
```

For a windowed count, "what it remembered" is a running count for every window that might still change. That memory is the **state store**. Here it's keyed by window and shop, and split into partitions like the shuffle, so each task owns the counts of its keys. Each batch writes its changes as a new version of the state in the query's checkpoint folder, which the fourth section comes back to.

Lesson 4's other window shapes use the same functions. `window(col("event_time"), "10 minutes", "5 minutes")` makes 10-minute windows that start every 5 minutes. Spark calls them sliding, and lesson 4 called them hopping. `session_window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes")` makes one window per burst of activity, ending after 5 quiet minutes.

The Try it replays lesson 4's processing-time trap in Spark. Then comes the question that drives the rest of this lesson: when is a window finished? Without an answer, Spark keeps every window's count forever, in case a late payment arrives. With 200,000 shops and 288 five-minute windows each a day, that's up to 57.6 million counts kept per day, growing until the executors run out of memory. And a count that may still change can't be written once, for good, into a table.

Next, we'll give Spark its answer: a watermark.

try.title: Count a backlog by arrival and by event time, in Spark
steps: Run `EventTimeDemo` from the `labs` folder. It makes up 30 minutes of payments for one shop, one every 20 seconds. The counting program is down from 10:10 to 10:20, and when it comes back it reads the waiting payments in about a minute. Spark then counts them per 5 minutes twice: by `arrival_time` and by `event_time`.
Predict the counts in the 10:10, 10:15 and 10:20 windows for both columns before you read them.
Which column would you put a fraud rule on, and what could still make that column's counts wrong?

code.title: EventTimeDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.stream.l08.demo

import org.apache.spark.sql.RowFactory
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.date_format
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import org.apache.spark.sql.types.DataTypes
import org.apache.spark.sql.types.StructType
import java.sql.Timestamp
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Merchant 7 gets one authorization every 20 seconds from 10:00 to 10:30. The fraud consumer is
 * down from 10:10 to 10:20; when it comes back it reads the backlog in about a minute. Counts per
 * 5 minutes, once by arrival (processing time) and once by when the card was used (event time).
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val outageStart = at("10:10")
    val outageEnd = at("10:20")
    val rows = (0 until 90).map { i ->
        val eventTime = at("10:00").plusSeconds(20L * i)
        val arrival = if (!eventTime.isBefore(outageStart) && eventTime.isBefore(outageEnd)) {
            // the backlog: 10 minutes of events read back in 1 minute, in order
            outageEnd.plusMillis(Duration.between(outageStart, eventTime).toMillis() / 10)
        } else {
            eventTime.plusSeconds(2)                                        // normally a 2-second lag
        }
        RowFactory.create(7, Timestamp.from(eventTime), Timestamp.from(arrival))
    }
    val schema = StructType().add("merchant_id", DataTypes.IntegerType)
        .add("event_time", DataTypes.TimestampType).add("arrival_time", DataTypes.TimestampType)
    val events = spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema)

    fun countBy(column: String) = events.groupBy(window(col(column), "5 minutes")).count()
        .select(date_format(col("window.start"), "HH:mm").alias("w"), col("count"))
        .collectAsList().associate { it.getString(0) to it.getLong(1) }
    val byArrival = countBy("arrival_time")
    val byEvent = countBy("event_time")
    println("window   by arrival time   by event time")
    for (w in (byArrival.keys + byEvent.keys).sorted()) {
        println("%-8s %10d %17d".format(w, byArrival[w] ?: 0, byEvent[w] ?: 0))
    }
    println("events: ${rows.size}; rule \"more than 30 in 5 minutes\" fires on arrival time: " +
        byArrival.filterValues { it > 30 }.keys + ", on event time: " + byEvent.filterValues { it > 30 }.keys)
    spark.stop()
}

try.expect:
```text
window   by arrival time   by event time
10:00            15                15
10:05            15                15
10:10             0                15
10:15             0                15
10:20            45                15
10:25            15                15
events: 90; rule "more than 30 in 5 minutes" fires on arrival time: [10:20], on event time: []
```

By arrival time, the outage shows up as two empty windows and a spike of 45 at 10:20, and the rule "more than 30 in 5 minutes" fires on it. By event time, every window has 15 payments, which is what really happened. The event-time count is only as good as the timestamps: a machine with a wrong clock, or one that stamps payments when it sends them instead of when the card was used, breaks it.

sections.h: Spark's watermark: the newest payment time minus a delay you choose
sections.body:
Lesson 4's answer was a watermark, and Spark works out the simplest kind. A **watermark** is Spark's running estimate of how far event time has got: "nothing older than this is still on its way". You set it with one line, on the event-time column, before the count:

```kotlin
events.withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
```

The rule is short. After each micro-batch, Spark takes the newest event time it has seen so far and subtracts the delay you gave. Newest 10:14, delay 10 minutes: the watermark is 10:04. The watermark only moves forward. A window is final once the watermark reaches its end, and then two things happen: its count can be written out, and its state is deleted. That deletion is what keeps the state store from growing forever.

Think of a teacher collecting homework, one pile per day. She doesn't close Monday's pile at midnight. She closes it once homework dated two days later starts arriving, betting that no Monday homework is later than that. The piles are windows, the dates are event times, and the two days are the delay. A quiet class brings no later homework, so its piles stay open. The picture breaks at the calendar. A teacher could close a pile because the date says so; Spark looks only at the times on the payments, never at a wall clock.

Three details catch people out, and the stepper shows each one.

First, the new watermark takes effect from the next batch. A payment that arrives in the same batch as a big jump in time is judged against the old watermark.

Second, Spark drops a late payment when its **window** has closed, not when the payment is older than the delay. In batch 3, a payment from 10:03 arrives 11 minutes behind the newest, more than the 10 minutes allowed, and it's still counted. Its window, 10:00 to 10:05, ends at 10:05, and the watermark is at 10:04. Spark's documentation promises only one direction: data less late than the delay is never dropped, and later data may or may not be counted.

Third, the watermark moves only when new payments arrive. If the stream goes quiet, the last windows wait, and their counts aren't written until later payments push the watermark past their ends.

The delay is a bet, and it trades two costs. A longer delay counts more late payments, keeps more windows in state and writes each final count later. A shorter one writes sooner and drops more. Choose it from data. Measure how late your payments really are, the gap between processing time and event time, and take a high percentile: a value that, say, 99.9% of the gaps stay under. Then watch `numRowsDroppedByWatermark`, a number in the progress report Spark writes after each batch, to see what the bet costs.

**Spark judges a late payment by its window's end, not by its age.** Next, we'll decide when and how each window's count leaves the query.

package sfz.stream.l08.demo

import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.VoidFunction2
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.date_format
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import java.io.File
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue

/**
 * A windowed count with a 10-minute watermark, in append mode. Six batches of events arrive, some
 * out of order and late. After each one, prints the watermark, what append mode wrote, how many
 * windows the state holds and how many events were dropped as too late.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val events = authorizations(spark)
    val written = ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String>()
    val query = events.toDF()
        .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
        .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"))
        .count()
        .select(date_format(col("window.start"), "HH:mm").alias("start"), date_format(col("window.end"), "HH:mm").alias("end"), col("count"))
        .writeStream()
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", File(DEMO_DIR, "watermark-checkpoint").absolutePath)
        // print-friendly sink: collect what each micro-batch writes
        .foreachBatch(VoidFunction2<Dataset<Row>, Long> { df, _ ->
            df.collectAsList().forEach { written += "[${it.getString(0)}, ${it.getString(1)}) = ${it.getLong(2)}" }
        })
        .start()

    var batch = 0
    fun step(vararg times: String) {
        val before = query.watermark()
        events.send(*times)
        query.processAllAvailable()
        val ops = query.recentProgress().flatMap { it.stateOperators().toList() }
        val dropped = ops.sumOf { it.numRowsDroppedByWatermark() }
        val inState = query.lastProgress().stateOperators().first().numRowsTotal()
        val out = generateSequence { written.poll() }.toList().sorted()
        println("batch ${++batch}: sent ${times.joinToString(" ")}")
        println("   watermark ${before} -> ${query.watermark()}; append wrote ${if (out.isEmpty()) "nothing" else out.joinToString()}; " +
            "windows in state: $inState; dropped so far: $dropped")
    }
    step("10:01", "10:02", "10:06")
    step("10:14")
    step("10:03")
    step("10:21")
    step("10:04", "10:08")
    step("10:13")
    query.stop()
    spark.stop()
}

Batch 4's 10:21 moves the watermark to 10:11, which closes two windows: append mode writes each exactly once, and the state drops from 3 windows to 2. refs.title: Structured Streaming: handling late data and watermarking

sections.h: Output modes: when each window's count is written, and how often
sections.body:
A windowed count is a result table that keeps changing. The sink is where the results go: a folder of files, a table, a Kafka log. The **output mode** says which rows of the result table each micro-batch hands to the sink. It's lesson 4's choice between writing a window once, when it's final, and writing it early, then correcting it.

Append mode writes a row once, when it can no longer change. For a windowed count, that means when the watermark closes the window. It's the only mode for sinks that can't change what they've written, such as files, and most paths into Iceberg. Iceberg is a table format. It keeps a table as Parquet files, which store data column by column, plus a list of snapshots saying which files make up the table. The Batch track's lakehouse lesson builds it. Append mode needs a watermark for any count, and its price is waiting: the 10:00 window appears only after a payment from 10:15 or later has arrived.

Update mode writes every row that changed in this batch, as soon as it changes. The fraud check sees "shop 7, window 10:00, count 2" right away, and "count 3" when the late payment arrives. That suits a sink that can upsert by key: insert a row if its key is new, and overwrite it if not. A key-value store, which keeps one value per key, does that. So does `MERGE`, an SQL command that inserts a row or updates the one already there, inside `foreachBatch`, a hook where your own code receives each batch's result and writes it wherever it likes. The watermark still cleans up the state.

Complete mode writes the whole result table every batch. It's for small results, such as a dashboard's top 10, and it can't drop state, because it has to write every window again every time. In the Try it, complete mode even counts a late 10:04 that the other two modes dropped, because it never removes a window from state.

The sink has to agree with the mode. Spark's file sink only appends. Iceberg's streaming sink supports append and complete. Kafka and `foreachBatch` take whatever you give them, and the rest is up to you.

For a fraud alert you want the earliest signal, so use update mode into a store keyed by shop and window. For the table people will study later, use append mode into Iceberg, so each window lands once, final.

Append mode writes each window once, as long as nothing crashes. Next, we'll crash the query between a write and Spark's note of that write.

refs.title: Structured Streaming: output modes and sinks

sections.h: Exactly-once needs a source that can replay, a checkpoint and a sink that ignores repeats
sections.body:
Lesson 7 said micro-batching gets exactly-once by saving each batch's output and its end offset together. Here is how Spark does it, and the part it leaves to you. Structured Streaming can give you exactly-once from the source to the sink, but only if three parts each do their share.

The source must be replayable: asking for the same records again must return the same records. Kafka is. Spark asks it for a range of offsets, and asking again later returns the same payments. Spark doesn't rely on the offsets a group of readers has committed in Kafka; it keeps its own.

The checkpoint folder records progress. Before a batch runs, Spark writes the batch's offset ranges to `offsets/<batch id>`. After the sink has written the batch, Spark writes `commits/<batch id>`. The state store's versions live in `state/`. On a restart, Spark finds the last batch with an offsets entry but no commit entry. It runs that batch again with the same offsets and state, so it produces the same output.

That replay is the catch. If the crash came after the sink wrote the batch but before `commits/` recorded it, the sink receives the same output twice. So the sink must be **idempotent**, meaning that writing the same batch twice leaves the same result as writing it once, or transactional. Spark's file sink and Iceberg's sink both are. Iceberg records the query's id and the batch id (`spark.sql.streaming.epochId`) in each snapshot's summary, and skips a batch it has already committed.

In `foreachBatch` you get the batch id, and you have to use it yourself: for example, a `MERGE` keyed on the window, or the batch id written next to the data. A plain `INSERT` is at-least-once. So is Spark's Kafka sink. The Try it fakes exactly that crash: the Parquet folder written by a naive `foreachBatch` ends with 4 rows, and the Iceberg table with 2.

This is the usual path from Kafka into a lakehouse, the files-plus-table-format home for data that people study later. A Structured Streaming job reads the topic, counts or cleans the payments, and appends to Iceberg every minute or so. Each batch is one commit, so a one-minute trigger makes 1,440 snapshots a day, plus at least one small file per partition for every batch that writes rows. Plan from day one to merge small files into big ones (compaction) and to delete old snapshots (expiry). The Batch track's lesson Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs shows how.

**A replayed batch writes the same rows again. Give it a sink that notices.** Next, we'll see what Spark gives up when it stops waiting for batches.

package sfz.stream.l08.demo

import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.VoidFunction2
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.StreamingQuery
import java.io.File

/**
 * One windowed count, written by two queries with their own checkpoints: one to an Iceberg table,
 * one through foreachBatch to a plain Parquet folder (append, ignoring the batch id). Then a
 * crash is faked between "the sink wrote" and "the commit log says so", and both restart.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val events = authorizations(spark)
    val counts = events.toDF()
        .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
        .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
        .count()
        .select(col("window.start").alias("window_start"), col("merchant_id"), col("count").alias("authorizations"))
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.auth_counts (window_start TIMESTAMP, merchant_id INT, authorizations BIGINT) USING iceberg")
    val icebergCheckpoint = File(DEMO_DIR, "checkpoint-iceberg")
    val folderCheckpoint = File(DEMO_DIR, "checkpoint-folder")
    val folder = File(DEMO_DIR, "auth-counts-parquet")

    fun startIceberg(): StreamingQuery = counts.writeStream().format("iceberg").outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", icebergCheckpoint.absolutePath).toTable("lake.pay.auth_counts")
    fun startFolder(): StreamingQuery = counts.writeStream().outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", folderCheckpoint.absolutePath)
        // a sink that is NOT idempotent: it appends whatever the batch holds, ignoring the batch id
        .foreachBatch(VoidFunction2<Dataset<Row>, Long> { df, _ -> df.write().mode("append").parquet(folder.absolutePath) })
        .start()
    fun rows(): String {
        val ice = spark.table("lake.pay.auth_counts").count()
        val par = if (folder.exists()) spark.read().parquet(folder.absolutePath).count() else 0
        return "Iceberg table $ice rows, Parquet folder $par rows"
    }
    fun logs(dir: File, name: String) = File(dir, name).list()!!.filter { !it.startsWith(".") }.map { it.toInt() }.sorted()

    var ice = startIceberg()
    var par = startFolder()
    for (b in listOf(listOf("10:01", "10:02", "10:06"), listOf("10:21"))) {
        events.send(*b.toTypedArray())
        ice.processAllAvailable()
        par.processAllAvailable()
    }
    println("before the crash: ${rows()}")
    println("checkpoint: offsets ${logs(icebergCheckpoint, "offsets")}, commits ${logs(icebergCheckpoint, "commits")}, " +
        "state/ holds ${File(icebergCheckpoint, "state").walkTopDown().count { it.isFile && it.name.endsWith(".delta") }} delta files")
    println("offsets/3 starts with: " + File(icebergCheckpoint, "offsets/3").readLines()[1].substringBefore(",\"conf\"") + "}")
    ice.stop()
    par.stop()

    // the crash: both sinks wrote batch 3, but the process died before the commit log recorded it
    for (dir in listOf(icebergCheckpoint, folderCheckpoint)) {
        val last = logs(dir, "commits").last()
        File(dir, "commits/$last").delete()
        File(dir, "commits/.$last.crc").delete()
    }
    println("deleted commits/3 in both checkpoints; restarting")
    ice = startIceberg()
    par = startFolder()
    ice.processAllAvailable()
    par.processAllAvailable()
    println("after the restart, Spark ran batch ${ice.recentProgress().first().batchId()} again: ${rows()}")
    println("Iceberg snapshots by epoch: " + spark.sql(
        "SELECT summary['spark.sql.streaming.epochId'] AS epoch, coalesce(summary['added-records'], '0') AS added " +
            "FROM lake.pay.auth_counts.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").collectAsList().joinToString { "${it.getString(0)}:+${it.getString(1)}" })
    ice.stop()
    par.stop()
    spark.stop()
}

try.expect:
```text
before the crash: Iceberg table 2 rows, Parquet folder 2 rows
checkpoint: offsets [0, 1, 2, 3], commits [0, 1, 2, 3], state/ holds 16 delta files
offsets/3 starts with: {"batchWatermarkMs":1794046260000,"batchTimestampMs":1794089660196}
deleted commits/3 in both checkpoints; restarting
after the restart, Spark ran batch 3 again: Iceberg table 2 rows, Parquet folder 4 rows
Iceberg snapshots by epoch: 0:+0, 1:+0, 2:+0, 3:+2
```

Before the crash, both sinks hold the same 2 rows: the windows 10:00 and 10:05, written in batch 3, a batch with no new payments that Spark ran to move the watermark. With `commits/3` gone, both queries ran batch 3 again with the same offsets and state, and produced the same 2 rows. The Parquet sink appended them a second time: 4 rows, two of them duplicates. The Iceberg sink saw that this query had already committed batch 3 (epoch 3 holds the only added records) and skipped it: still 2 rows. Spark also committed an Iceberg snapshot for each empty batch. `offsets/3` stores the batch's watermark (`batchWatermarkMs`, in milliseconds since 1970), so the replay closes exactly the windows the first run closed.

sections.h: Real-time mode removes the micro-batch floor, and its Kafka sink is at-least-once
sections.body:
Micro-batches put a floor under the delay. Spark's guide gives about 100 ms from input to output, because every batch pays for planning and starting its tasks. Spark 4.1 added **real-time mode** to remove that floor. Spark 4.3 extended it from queries that keep no state to ones that do: removing duplicates, and aggregations such as counts, windowed ones included. It also added `transformWithState` for Java and Kotlin code, which keeps your own state per key (see Go deeper). The labs use Spark 4.1 and have no Kafka connection, so this section has no demo to run.

The change is in how tasks run. Instead of a new set of tasks for every batch, real-time mode starts **long-running tasks, one per input partition**, that handle records as they arrive. The docs describe the delay from input to output dropping from the micro-batch floor to roughly the time it takes to process and send one record, often a few milliseconds. You turn it on with a trigger, and the duration in it is not a delay target:

```kotlin
counts.writeStream()
    .format("kafka")
    .outputMode("update")                                // required in real-time mode
    .trigger(Trigger.RealTime("5 minutes"))              // a checkpoint interval: commit progress every 5 min
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake-checkpoints/fraud-rt")
    .start()
```

A "batch" still exists. It's 5 minutes long by default, and 5 seconds at the least, and at its end Spark commits offsets and state. That turns lesson 7's micro-batch trade around. The built-in Kafka sink writes results as records arrive, while the input offsets are committed only at the end of the batch. So a failure partway through a batch replays the batch from its start, and can write up to a whole batch of output again. The docs are explicit: the state is exactly-once, the Kafka sink is at-least-once, and real-time mode has no exactly-once sink yet. Programs reading that topic must remove the repeats themselves, for example on a key built from the shop and the window.

The rest of the fine print shapes what you can build. The source must be Kafka. The sinks are Kafka, `foreach`, the console and memory: no `foreachBatch`, so no Iceberg. Joins of two streams, session windows and adaptive query execution (Spark re-planning a query while it runs) aren't supported. A join with a fixed table must send a copy of that table to every task. It needs the RocksDB state store, which keeps state in files on local disk. And it needs a core, one processor of a machine, for every task, all the time. A 10-partition topic feeding a count with 5 shuffle partitions needs at least 15 cores.

Here are the engines of this track side by side. Kafka Streams has no separate watermark: it uses stream time, the newest timestamp it has seen, minus a grace period (lesson 5).

| Engine | Unit of work | How event time moves on | Getting through a crash | Exactly-once into Kafka |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kafka Streams | one record, inside your own program | stream time minus a grace period | changelog topics plus transactions | yes, `exactly_once_v2` |
| Flink | one record | watermarks | barrier checkpoints | yes, with a transactional sink |
| Spark micro-batch | one batch, about 100 ms and up | a watermark per batch | checkpoint folder, batch replay | no: readers remove repeats |
| Spark real-time mode | one record, in long-running tasks | a watermark | one commit per long batch | no: at-least-once sink |

Choose by what you already run and what the job needs. Kafka Streams fits programs that already live on Kafka. Flink fits when streaming is the product: very large state, a result for each record within milliseconds, many jobs that run for months. Spark fits a team that already runs it for batch work and writes to lakehouse tables. Its delay is seconds, or milliseconds in real-time mode if repeats in the Kafka output are acceptable.

All four engines answer questions about the last few minutes, close their windows, and drop what comes too late. A question about all of last year's payments has a different shape: its input is complete before the job starts.

try.title: Size a real-time query and its replay
steps: A fraud query reads `card-authorizations`, a topic with 24 partitions. It counts with `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=8`, so 8 tasks after the shuffle, and writes alerts to Kafka in real-time mode with `Trigger.RealTime("2 minutes")`. How many cores must the cluster, the group of machines Spark runs on, give this query at the least?
The query fails 90 seconds into a batch and restarts. Which alerts can the programs reading them see twice?
What would you change in the program that reads the alerts, and why not shorten the trigger to 5 seconds instead?
try.expect: At least 32 cores: 24 long-running reader tasks, one per partition, plus 8 tasks for the count after the shuffle, all running at once (the docs' sizing rule; run one real-time query per cluster). After the failure, Spark restarts the batch from its committed offsets, so alerts written in those 90 seconds can be written again: the Kafka sink is at-least-once. Make the reader idempotent, keyed on the shop and the window. A 5-second trigger shrinks the replay, but it commits offsets and state every 5 seconds, and it still doesn't make the sink exactly-once.

mistake: The common mistake is putting the watermark on the wrong thing, or leaving it out. Without `withWatermark`, a windowed count in update or complete mode runs fine in testing. Then, in real use, it keeps every window of every shop in state forever, until the executors run out of memory weeks later. With the watermark on a different column from the window, or added after the count, Spark can't use it to close windows, and it refuses to start an append-mode query. People make this mistake because the batch version of the same query needs no watermark, so the streaming version looks complete without one. The fix: call `withWatermark` on the same event-time column the window uses, before the `groupBy`; choose the delay from measured lateness; and watch two numbers in the query's progress report, the rows in state (they should level off) and `numRowsDroppedByWatermark` (it should stay small).

worked.title: From a Kafka topic to an Iceberg table of fraud counts

steps.say: Read the topic. Kafka hands over bytes, so turn each message's value from JSON text into columns, and keep the payment's own timestamp, `authorized_at`, as the event time. `startingOffsets` applies only to the very first run; after that, the checkpoint folder decides where to start.
steps.code:
val raw = spark.readStream()
    .format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "card-authorizations")
    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
    .load()
val events = raw.select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), AUTH_SCHEMA).alias("a"))
    .select(col("a.merchant_id"), col("a.authorized_at").alias("event_time"))

steps.say: Count by event time, with a watermark on the same column, before the count. The delay comes from measured lateness. Here (made-up numbers), 99.9% of payments arrived within about 6 minutes of their event time, so 10 minutes leaves room.
steps.code:
val counts = events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
    .select(col("window.start").alias("window_start"), col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
        col("merchant_id"), col("count").alias("authorizations"))

steps.say: Write final windows once, into Iceberg. Append mode plus Iceberg's batch-id check gives exactly-once. A one-minute trigger means one commit, and one Iceberg snapshot, a minute instead of one every few seconds.

Watch it. Each micro-batch reports its watermark, the rows in state and the rows dropped as late. Send them to whatever charts you watch: state that keeps growing means the watermark isn't cleaning up, and a rising drop count means the delay is too short.
steps.code:
val p = query.lastProgress()
log.info("watermark={} stateRows={} droppedLate={}",
    p.eventTime()["watermark"],
    p.stateOperators()[0].numRowsTotal(),
    p.stateOperators()[0].numRowsDroppedByWatermark())

lab.title: Model the watermark, then run it against Spark
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All eleven fail on `TODO`s. `WindowedCounterTest` checks your model on its own. `AuthorizationCountsTest` drives a real Spark stream from a `MemoryStream`, so the tests choose exactly which payments form each micro-batch and no Kafka is needed. It writes to an Iceberg table in a temporary folder.

Write `WindowedCounter`. `windowOf` rounds a time down to the start of its 5-minute window. `batch` drops payments whose window ends at or before the current watermark, counts the rest, moves the watermark to the newest event time minus the delay (never back), and emits and forgets the windows that end at or before it.

Write `AuthorizationCounts.perWindow`: the watermark, the window, the count, then split the window into two columns, `window_start` and `window_end`. Write `start`: append mode, the checkpoint folder and the Iceberg sink.

The last test feeds the same seven batches to your model and to Spark, and checks that they agree on every watermark, every window written and the number of payments dropped. If they disagree, the failing batch tells you which rule is off.
Read the replay test. It deletes the newest `commits/` file, starts the query again and expects no duplicate rows. Which part of the system makes that pass?
hints: Window start: `Instant.ofEpochMilli(ms - Math.floorMod(ms, size.toMillis()))`. A `TreeMap<Instant, Long>` keyed by window start makes the state, and `headMap(watermark.minus(size), true)` gives the windows that are closed.
Keep the newest event time across batches in a field. Check each payment against the watermark from before the batch, then update the watermark.
lab.done_when: All eleven tests in `WindowedCounterTest` and `AuthorizationCountsTest` pass.

drill.title: A watermarked count from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Structured Streaming query that counts payments per shop (`merchant_id`) in 5-minute event-time windows, accepts payments up to 15 minutes late, and appends final windows to the Iceberg table `lake.fraud.velocity`. Then answer: with the newest payment at 11:40, is a payment from 11:24 counted? One from 11:26?

answer.src:
events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")        // same column as the window, before groupBy
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
    .writeStream()
    .format("iceberg")
    .outputMode("append")                            // each window once, when final
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/velocity")
    .toTable("lake.fraud.velocity")

// latest event 11:40, so the watermark is 11:25 (from the next batch on).
// 11:24 is in [11:20, 11:25), which ends at 11:25 <= watermark: closed, dropped.
// 11:26 is in [11:25, 11:30), which ends after 11:25: still open, counted.

recap: Structured Streaming is lesson 7's micro-batching on Spark's batch engine: each batch runs your query on the new input and folds the result into a state store, saved in the query's checkpoint folder. Count by event time, or catching up after an outage looks like a spike.

The watermark is the newest event time seen minus the delay you allow. A window is final once the watermark reaches its end: its count is written and its state deleted, and later payments for it are dropped.
Spark drops a late payment by its window's end, not by its own age, and a new watermark applies from the next batch. Data less late than the delay is never dropped.
Append writes each row once, when final; update writes the rows that changed; complete writes everything every time and never drops state. The sink must support the mode.
Exactly-once needs a replayable source, the checkpoint folder and an idempotent or transactional sink. Iceberg skips a replayed batch by its id; a plain `INSERT` in `foreachBatch` doesn't.

The limits: real-time mode (Spark 4.1, with state since 4.3) gets milliseconds from long-running tasks, but its Kafka sink is at-least-once, so a failure can write a whole batch of output again. And every engine here answers questions about recent data: a window closes, and what comes too late is dropped.
closing:
We started with a payment stamped 10:03 that turned up at 10:14. Spark counted it, because its window ends at 10:05 and the watermark had only reached 10:04. Its window decided, not its age.

If a watch or phone counts your steps, check yesterday's total after the watch has been out of range and syncs again. The total can still go up: each step carries its own time, and the app keeps yesterday's window open for latecomers.

Next, we'll start the Batch processing and analytics track, where the input is complete before the job begins. We'll ask how long reading all of it takes, and whether you need more than one machine.

quiz.q: A team moves a fraud query to Spark 4.3's real-time mode with `Trigger.RealTime("5 minutes")`, writing alerts to Kafka. The query fails 4 minutes into a batch and restarts. What can the programs that read the alert topic see?
options: Each alert exactly once, because real-time mode is exactly-once
A 4-minute gap of missing alerts
Nothing new until the batch commits, as in a micro-batch query
Alerts from those 4 minutes written a second time
quiz.why: Real-time mode writes alerts as records arrive, and the input offsets are committed only at the end of each batch. After the failure, Spark starts again from the last committed offsets, so the records of those 4 minutes are processed again and their alerts written again. The state is exactly-once; the built-in Kafka sink is at-least-once. Nothing is lost, and the output isn't held back until the commit, which is the whole point of the mode.

quiz.q: A team's streaming count runs in update mode with no `withWatermark`. Tests pass. What happens in real use over the following weeks?
options: Nothing: update mode writes each change, so it doesn't need state
Late payments get dropped after a default 10-minute watermark
Every window of every shop stays in the state store forever, so the state and each checkpoint grow until the executors run short of memory
Spark refuses to start the query
quiz.why: Without a watermark, Spark can never decide that a window is final, so it keeps every count in case a late payment arrives. Update mode still needs the state to know the new count. There is no default watermark. Spark refuses append mode for a count without a watermark, but update and complete start fine, which is why this slips through tests.

quiz.q: Which sink gives exactly-once results when Spark replays a batch after a crash?
options: The Iceberg sink, or a `foreachBatch` that does a `MERGE` keyed on window and shop
`foreachBatch` that runs `INSERT INTO shop_counts SELECT * FROM batch`
The Kafka sink
Any sink, because the checkpoint guarantees exactly-once by itself
quiz.why: After a crash, Spark runs the last uncommitted batch again with the same offsets and state. Iceberg records the query and batch id in each snapshot and skips a batch it has already committed, and a `MERGE` keyed on the window overwrites the same values. A plain `INSERT` appends the batch twice, and Spark's Kafka sink is at-least-once. The checkpoint makes the replay repeat itself exactly, but the sink decides whether the repeat shows.

quiz.q: A dashboard must show the current count of the open 5-minute window, changing as payments arrive. The sink is a key-value store keyed by shop and window. Which output mode fits?
options: Append, because it is exactly-once
Update, because it writes each changed window right away and the sink can overwrite by key
Complete, because the dashboard needs every window
Any of them: output modes only change speed
quiz.why: Append writes a window only after the watermark closes it, which is minutes too late for a live count. Update writes each window whenever its count changes, and a store keyed by shop and window turns each write into an overwrite. Complete would write every window ever seen on every batch and never clean up its state.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: a Spark micro-batch query and a Flink job each crash and restart. Which is true of both?
options: Neither replays anything: both save each record's result before reading the next
Spark replays the last batch, while Flink's barriers mean nothing is ever replayed
Both replay input from saved offsets, and only an idempotent or transactional sink keeps repeats out of the output
Both drop the records that were in flight at the crash, which keeps the output exactly-once
quiz.why: Spark runs again the last batch that has an `offsets/` entry but no `commits/` entry. Flink restores the last completed checkpoint and rewinds its sources to the offsets in it. Either way, records are processed again. The state comes back consistent, but whether the outside world sees repeats depends on the sink: Iceberg's batch-id check or Flink's two-phase commit Kafka sink, against a plain insert.

flashcards.front: What does Spark's real-time mode change, and what does it not promise?
flashcards.back: Long-running tasks, one per input partition, handle records as they arrive: milliseconds instead of a floor of about 100 ms. The trigger's duration is the checkpoint interval. The state is exactly-once, but the built-in Kafka sink is at-least-once.

flashcards.front: How does Spark work out the watermark?
flashcards.back: The newest event time seen so far minus the delay given to `withWatermark`. It only moves forward, and a new value applies from the next micro-batch.
When the watermark reaches its end. Then append mode writes it once, and Spark deletes its state.

flashcards.front: Which late payments does Spark drop?
flashcards.back: Those whose window has already closed (window end at or before the watermark). A payment older than the delay is still counted if its window is open.

flashcards.front: What does each output mode write?
flashcards.back: Append: each row once, when final. Update: the rows changed in this batch. Complete: the whole result table every batch, with no state cleanup.

flashcards.front: What three things make a stream exactly-once from end to end?
flashcards.back: A replayable source (Kafka offsets), a checkpoint folder (offsets, commits, state), and an idempotent or transactional sink.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't a replayed batch duplicate rows in an Iceberg sink?
flashcards.back: Each Iceberg snapshot records the query id and the batch (epoch) id, and the sink skips a batch it has already committed.

terms.plain: When the event happened, such as when the card was used, as stamped in the event itself.
Spark's way of running a stream with long-running tasks that handle records as they arrive (Spark 4.1, with state since 4.3).
Back-to-back time slices of one size that don't overlap, such as every 5 minutes from 10:00.
One run of the streaming query over the input that arrived since the last run.
The running values Spark keeps per key between micro-batches, such as a count per window, saved in the checkpoint folder.
The newest event time seen minus an allowed delay; windows that end at or before it are final.
Which result rows each micro-batch writes: append, update or complete.
Where a query records its offsets, its finished batches and its state, so a restart carries on exactly.

explain_back.prompt: A friend asks why one shop's fraud count jumped at 10:20 in someone else's report and stayed flat in yours. Explain event time, the watermark and the late payment at 10:03 that was still counted, using the stepper's batches.
explain_back.answer: Their version counted payments by when the program read them. The program was down from 10:10 to 10:20 and read the waiting payments in a minute, so 10 minutes of payments landed in the 10:20 window, and the rule saw 45 in 5 minutes. Ours counts each payment in the window of its own timestamp, when the card was used, so the backlog went back to the 10:10 and 10:15 windows where it belongs. Event time raises a new question: when is a window finished, if a late payment can always turn up? The watermark answers it. After each micro-batch, Spark takes the newest event time seen and subtracts our allowed delay of 10 minutes. Every window that ends at or before that is final: Spark writes its count once and deletes its state, which keeps memory from growing. When 10:14 arrived, the watermark became 10:04. Then 10:03 arrived, 11 minutes behind 10:14, and it was still counted, because Spark drops a late payment only when its window has closed, and 10:00 to 10:05 ends at 10:05, after the watermark. When 10:21 arrived, the watermark moved to 10:11 and the first two windows were written. Payments for them that came afterwards, like 10:04 and 10:08, were dropped and counted in the drop number, which tells us whether 10 minutes was a good bet.

deeper.body:
Joins between two streams (lesson 6) need watermarks on both sides. To join payments with the later step that moves the money, both carrying `payment_id`, Spark keeps each side's rows in state until a match arrives. Add a watermark to each side and a time condition to the join (`capture_time BETWEEN auth_time AND auth_time + INTERVAL 7 DAYS`), and Spark can drop rows that can no longer find a match. Without them, the join's state grows forever, like the count without a watermark.

For logic per key that SQL can't express, such as "flag a card after three declines followed by an approval within 2 minutes", Spark 4.0 added `transformWithState`. You write a processor per key with typed state (single values, lists, maps), timers, and a time limit after which each piece of state expires. It's the closest Spark gets to Flink's keyed process functions.

State size matters in every engine. Spark's default state store keeps state in executor memory and writes changes to the checkpoint folder; the RocksDB state store keeps it on local disk and copes with much more. Flink 2.0's disaggregated state goes further and keeps the main copy on remote storage, so a job with terabytes of state can change its number of machines without moving it all.

*Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 12, describes micro-batching and checkpointing side by side; lessons 4 and 7 of this track build the same ideas from their original papers and docs.
